questions.question: What does display: flex do?
options: It turns the element into a flex container; direct children become flex items.
questions.explanation: Applying display: flex to an element turns it into a flex container, and its direct children turn into flex items.

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant
reference.excerpt: Applying display: flex to an element turns it into a flex container, and its direct children turn into flex items.

questions.question: Default flex direction is?
questions.explanation: By default, flex items align side by side, left to right, all in one row.

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant
reference.excerpt: By default, flex items align side by side, left to right, all in one row.

questions.question: Does the flex container fill the width?
options: No; it shrinks to content like an inline element.
Yes; it fills the available width like a block element.
Never; flex items fill it instead, always.
questions.explanation: The flex container fills the available width like a block element, but the flex items may not necessarily fill the width of their flex container.

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant
reference.excerpt: The flex container fills the available width like a block element, but the flex items may not necessarily fill the width of their flex container.

questions.question: display: inline-flex is for?
options: A flex container that behaves more like inline-block.
questions.explanation: inline-flex creates a flex container that behaves more like an inline-block element rather than a block.

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant
reference.excerpt: You can also use display: inline-flex. This creates a flex container that behaves more like an inline-block element rather than a block.

questions.question: Flex layout is defined in terms of?
options: A main axis and a cross axis.
questions.explanation: Because flexbox layout is defined in terms of the main axis and cross axis, I'll use the terms start and end in reference to the axes.

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant
reference.excerpt: Main axis Cross axis 5.1 Flex container 1 2 Flex items 3 4 Figure 5.1 A flexbox container and its elements The items are placed along a line called the main axis, which goes from the main-start (left) to the main-end (right).

questions.question: You need all twelve new properties to use flexbox?
options: No. display: flex gets you pretty far before you need the rest.
You need exactly twelve or it does nothing.
questions.explanation: Applying display: flex gets you pretty far before you'll need to pick up any of those 12 new properties.

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant
reference.excerpt: The rest of the properties provide options for aligning and spacing elements.

questions.question: justify-content packs items along?
questions.explanation: Chapter coverage includes element alignment. justify-content is the main-axis packing property.

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant
reference.excerpt: Perpendicular to the main axis is the cross axis. This goes from the cross-start (top) to the cross-end (bottom).

questions.question: align-items packs items along?
questions.explanation: Cross-axis alignment is align-items (center, stretch, flex-start, ...).

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant
reference.excerpt: Main axis Cross axis 5.1 Flex container 1 2 Flex items 3 4 Figure 5.1 A flexbox container and its elements The items are placed along a line called the main axis, which goes from the main-start (left) to the main-end (right).

questions.question: How can you push the last menu item to the right?
options: An auto left margin on that item.
text-align: right on the li text only.
questions.explanation: An auto left margin on the last button fills available space, pushing it to the right.

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant
reference.excerpt: You’ll also apply an auto left margin to the last button, which causes the margin to fill all the available space, pushing the last button all the way to the right.

questions.question: flex: 1 on an item typically means?
options: The item fills remaining space on the main axis.
The item becomes a grid container.
questions.explanation: Grant's figure: second item with flex: 1 fills all remaining space.

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant
reference.excerpt: The flex items are all the same height, determined naturally by their contents.

questions.question: flex: none means?
options: The item stays at its natural size and does not grow.
The container is not a flex container.
questions.explanation: Items with flex: none grow to their natural width. They don't necessarily fill the container.

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant
reference.excerpt: Add the following to your stylesheet. Listing 5.7 Using the flex property to set column widths .column-main { flex: 2; } .column-sidebar { flex: 1; } Now the two columns grow to fill the space, so together they are the same width as the nav bar, with the main column twice as wide as the sidebar.

questions.question: Are flex items the same height by default?
options: No; each is its own content height with no stretching.
Yes; they are all the same height, determined naturally by their contents.
questions.explanation: The flex items are all the same height, determined naturally by their contents.

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant
reference.excerpt: Flex items within it generally behave the same as with display: flex.

questions.question: Why did floats struggle with equal-height columns that flexbox handles?
options: Flex items share height in a row by default; floats do not.
questions.explanation: Flexbox is a simple solution to the long-standing problems of vertical centering and equal height columns.

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant
reference.excerpt: I’ll cover a few basic principles of the flexbox layout that you’ll need to understand, followed by practical examples.

questions.question: Which rule spaces items without putting margin on the outer edges, Grant's sibling trick?
questions.explanation: margin-left plus an adjacent sibling combinator puts space between items, not on the outside edges.

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant
reference.excerpt: You can achieve this layout by using the margin-left property and an adjacent sibling combinator, which is a method similar to the lobotomized owl from chapter 3.
